etween the Helleren and Egersund--Ogna bodies, lies the smaller Haaland anorthosite intrusion; 7 sites (62--68) are distributed along the length of this body (Fig. 2). Magnetic properties are similar to the Aana-Sira Massif and cores from the majority of sites (57-62 and 65) were magnetised in WNW directions with very steep negative inclinations which remained stable to the limits of a.f. treatment; in general, there is no appreciable movement of the remanence vector during cleaning, although vectors from cores at sites 57 and 59 moved continuously through a few degrees of arc in a southerly direction. Two sites (67 and 68) with low coercivity components become less stable in higher a.f. fields, but yield comparable directions in low a.f. fields (Table V). Sites 63, 64 and 66 are magnetised with directions ~ 40 ° shallower and are excluded from the group mean calculation. The Bjerkrem--Sogndal lopolith This lopolith was intruded in 4 phases exposed around the margin of the Aana-Sira Massif and north of the Helleren and Egersund--Ogna bodies (Fig. 2). The earliest phase of anorthosite and norite is exposed in 3 areas. The larger two, in the vicinity of Bjerkrem (58°36'N 6°5'E) and Sogndal, were sampled at sites 74, 75, 79--81 and at sites 71--73, 76, respectively. The

In addition, the blocking temperature spectra of rocks from the southern part of the farsundite body are higher than those within the northern limb of the intrusion. In both cases the implied direction of a.p.w, is away from the sam- pling locality (Fig. 7). Since the rate of cooling of the migmatites surrounding the igneous com- plex is approximately known, as are the blocking temperatures of the rock samples, it is possible to estimate the rate of a.p.w, represented by the swathe in Fig. 7. Samples from the farsundite body yielding mean unblocking temperatures of 520 and 570°C have palaeopoles separated by an angular distance of 35 ° and imply an a.p.w, rate of 3 ° Ma -1. In the Aana-Sira Massif a set of samples with mean unblocking temperature of 590°C yield a pole separated by 8 ° from a set of samples in the Bjerkrem--Sogudal lopolith with a mean unblocking temperature of 565 °, implying an a.p.w, rate of 1.3 ° Ma -1. These estimates are appreciably higher than most Phanerozoic rates, but appear to be fairly typical of the Phanerozoic era (Piper, 1981, 1982). Thus, the collective poles of this study which define a swathe of ~30 ° in length appear to represent 10--20 Ma of a.p.w, movement. The width of the distribution

Although we have been unable to correct for shape aniso- tropy, the effect of this is believed to be small for two reasons: in the farsun- dite body with strong visible anisotropy the greatest apparent deflection of the remanent vector by this effect was found to be 5.5 ° and to average 3.2 ° (Murthy and Deutsch, 1975). Secondly, the rocks of the Bjerkrem--Sogndal lopolith are folded, but no significant correlation has been found here be- tween the direction of dip of the layers of the lopolith and the direction of magnetisation. The palaeopoles from the farsundite body are slightly displaced from the almost parallel swathe defined by the anorthosite complex (Fig. 7). This is one discrepancy which may have a tectonic explanation because the farsun- dite lies adjacent to the North Sea margin: a southerly tilting of ~10 ° along the coastal margin here could accommodate the difference between the mag- netic vectors in this body and the anorthosite complexes. A sampling site comprises a minimum of 7 cores distributed over several metres of outcrop and drilled with a portable drilling motor of the kind de- scribed by Doell and Cox (1967). Cores were orientated by sights on the Sun or, in the limited number of cases where this was not possible, by magnetic bearings in conjunction with topographic sights. The cores were sliced in the laboratory and measured with an automated parastatic magnetometer system. Alternating field (a.f.) demagnetisation is most suitable for analysing the broad range of coercivities present in the (predominantly magnetite-held) remanences in these rocks and was utilised in increments of 5 or 10 mT (milliTesla) as the standard method of treatment for this collection. In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). Although the coercivity spectrum cannot of course be directly linked to the blocking temperature spectrum, similar behaviours are observed with both a.f. and thermal techniques in samples with broad spec- tra (Morgan, 1976a, b; Piper, 1981) so that the phenomenon can, at least in some rocks, be recovered by both methods. In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). Although the coercivity spectrum cannot of course be directly linked to the blocking temperature spectrum, similar behaviours are observed with both a.f. and thermal techniques in samples with broad spec- tra (Morgan, 1976a, b; Piper, 1981) so that the phenomenon can, at least in some rocks, be recovered by both methods. Recognition of these effects re- quires that components illustrating them are shown to have a singular and primary origin (Piper, 1981). In principle, the acquisition of magnetisations in plutonic terrains should have been sufficiently slow to average out the effects of secular variation and, at any given crustal level, samples with higher blocking temperatures should record earlier parts of the a.p.w, path from those with lower block- ing temperatures. In addition, if the range of critical blocking temperatures is distributed, demagnetisation should recover progressively higher blocking temperatures and, therefore, older segments of the total magnetisations so that sample directions move progressively back along the a.p.w, path (Morgan, 1976a, b). Origin of magnetization The NE and SE magnetizations, which are characterized generally by a high coercitive force (h.c.f.) and a high blocking temperature, contain both normal (N) and reverse (R) polarities. The R polarities (SE, shallow positive) are always present in the h.c.f, region of AF demagnetization and this im- plies that the reverse SE component has its memory mainly in fine-grained magnetite. There are a few (2 or 3) exceptions to this rule and then the normal (NW, shallow negative) component is isolated in the h.c.f, region (see for instance specimen G8--1.3 in Table III). This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of amphibolite and granulite facies base- ment rocks across a 60 km wide north--south traverse through the Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt in West Greenland, which incorporates the c. 2500 Ma Itivdleq shear belt, the c. 1800 Ma Ikert6q shear belt, and adjoining terrains. It also integrates the results with earlier investigations of the belt to produce a composite record of the magnetic field during uplift and cooling of the terrain through c. 600--500°C at c. 1750--1600 Ma. Progressive a.f. and thermal cleaning of samples from 81 sites identifies a range of magnetic components. Lowest blocking temperature remanences in Nagssugtoqidian (c. 1700 Ma) amphibolite facies rocks yield steep W to N positive components residing in magnetite. Granulite facies rocks formed at c. 1800 Ma generally have a dual record incor- porating steep N to NW positive components unblocked by 580°C and shallow E--W di- rected components of dual polarity only unblocked close to the Curie point of haematite. V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of amphibolite and granulite facies base- ment rocks across a 60 km wide north--south traverse through the Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt in West Greenland, which incorporates the c. 2500 Ma Itivdleq shear belt, the c. 1800 Ma Ikert6q shear belt, and adjoining terrains. It also integrates the results with earlier investigations of the belt to produce a composite record of the magnetic field during uplift and cooling of the terrain through c. 600--500°C at c. 1750--1600 Ma. Progressive a.f. and thermal cleaning of samples from 81 sites identifies a range of magnetic components. Lowest blocking temperature remanences in Nagssugtoqidian (c. 1700 Ma) amphibolite facies rocks yield steep W to N positive components residing in magnetite. Granulite facies rocks formed at c. 1800 Ma generally have a dual record incor- porating steep N to NW positive components unblocked by 580°C and shallow E--W di- rected components of dual polarity only unblocked close to the Curie point of haematite. V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

Granulite facies rocks formed at c. 1800 Ma generally have a dual record incor- porating steep N to NW positive components unblocked by 580°C and shallow E--W di- rected components of dual polarity only unblocked close to the Curie point of haematite. V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

V. 76 INTRODUCTION The Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt, a zone of Archaean gneisses reworked during Proterozoic times, is exposed in both East and West Greenland, and is presumed to have an arcuate form around the northern margin of the South Greenland Archaean nucleus (Bridgwater et al., 1973). In West Green land it is both well exposed and accessible and has been the subject of palaeomagnetic endeavour by a number of workers, firstly to investigate the effect of slow uplift-related cooling on the acquisition of magnetic remanence in plutonic rocks (Morgan, 1976a, b; Beckmann et al., 1977: Piper, 1981), and secondly to elucidate the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) record during the lower-middle Proterozoic consolidation of this terrain (Beckmann and Mitchell, 1976; Fahrig and Bridgwater, 1976; Beckmann, 1979). The present study reports results of a detailed regional palaeomag- netic sample across the Nagssugtoqidian belt in West Greenland with the broad objectives of (1) resolving the magnetic record from the different metamorphic facies and tectonic zones, (2) linking together into a time sequence with the separate magnetisations identified from this and earlier studies, and (3) bringing together collective results from the Nagssugtoqidian terrain in Greenland to analyse them in the

Paleomagnetic techniques From each oriented sample, at least one stan- dard paleomagnetic specimen was prepared. The natural remanence of these samples was measured using a Schonstedt DSM-1 spinner magnetometer. Some specimens were subjected to alternating field (AF) demagnetization in steps, (typically 14) up to the maximum avail- able field of 100 mT using 2 and 3 axis instru- ments. Other specimens were subjected to thermal demagnetization, using a Schonstedt TSD-1 furnace, up to maximum temperatures of 700°C. In the thermal demagnetization experiments, the number of separate heatings and coolings followed by remanence measure- ment, varied between eight and 13 depending upon the ultimate unblocking temperatures. A few specimens were subjected to AF demagne- tization followed by thermal demagnetization. No 'blanket cleaning' procedures were used. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. These data appear to be in fair accordance with geological evidence. It should be noted, however, that the data and interpretations are of a preliminary nature and will no doubt change as the data base is expanded and improved. They do suggest, how- ever, that palaeomagnetic and magnetostratigraphic data have great poten- tial for resolving problems in Precambrian stratigraphy and tectonics. teristics provide impor- tant data relating to the sequential history of the Earth's magnetic field and the relative positions of crustal blocks. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. teristics provide impor- tant data relating to the sequential history of the Earth's magnetic field and the relative positions of crustal blocks. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. teristics provide impor- tant data relating to the sequential history of the Earth's magnetic field and the relative positions of crustal blocks. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: OCKS IN EASTERN CHINA Palaeomagnetism has emerged as an important tool in tectonic studies, particularly those concerned with ancient plate tectonics. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In this paper middle and upper Proterozoic (1900--1600 Ma) APW paths are presented for North and South China based on palaeomagnetic results obtained from the Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and Fuzhou areas in eastern China. Two or three "loops" are present; the second of these has an age of about 1000--800 Ma and is probably roughly equivalent to the Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops. APW paths, loops, reversed polari- ty zones and pole positions, combined with geological data, permit definition of several markers that are useful in regional correlation. These form the basis for a proposed strati- graphic subdivision of the middle and upper Proterozoic in China. A tentative palaeogeo- graphic map has been drawn for the North China and Yangzi Blocks for the period fr

- tematic studies of late Precambrian rocks ranging in age from 1900 Ma to 600 Ma. These studies have been carried out at Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and in the Fuzhou area where there is good exposure and the structure is relatively simple. These sections are suitable for measurement of remanent magnetization in the rocks. They are also the stratotype and para- stratotype sections for middle and upper Proterozoic rocks in China (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang, Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Zigiang et al., 1980; Chen Jinbiao et al,, 1981). 0301-9268/85/$03.30 © 1985 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. These data appear to be in fair accordance with geological evidence. It should be noted, however, that the data and interpretations are of a preliminary nature and will no doubt change as the data base is expanded and improved. They do suggest, how- ever, that palaeomagnetic and magnetostratigraphic data have great poten- tial for resolving problems in Precambrian stratigraphy and tectonics. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. These data appear to be in fair accordance with geological evidence. It should be noted, however, that the data and interpretations are of a preliminary nature and will no doubt change as the data base is expanded and improved. They do suggest, how- ever, that palaeomagnetic and magnetostratigraphic data have great poten- tial for resolving problems in Precambrian stratigraphy and tectonics. CONCLUSIONS In this paper we have used palaeomagnetic data to facilitate middle and upper Proterozoic stratigraphic correlations and relationships between North 75 China and Yangzi blocks in eastern China. It should be noted, however, that the data and interpretations are of a preliminary nature and will no doubt change as the data base is expanded and improved. The record of magnetization in the Precambrian can potentially provide data comparable to those provided by fossil metazoa in the Phanerozoic. In fact the study of remanent magnetiza- tion is complex because of superimposed influences of dlatsrophism, mag- matism and other thermal events throughout the long intervals of geologic time. In general, the older the rocks, the more complex the history is likely to be. Studies of APW paths, especially "loops", pole positions, palaeolatitudes and reversed polarity zones, taken in conjunction with geochronological palaeontological and geological data (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Ziqiang et al., 1980), suggest that a few magnetostrati- graphic marker beds might be present. Palaeomagnetic data, late Precambrian magnetostrati- graphy and tectonic evolution of eastern China. Precambrian Res., 29:65--75. In this paper middle and upper Proterozoic (1900--1600 Ma) APW paths are presented for North and South China based on palaeomagnetic results obtained from the Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and Fuzhou areas in eastern China. Two or three "loops" are present; the second of these has an age of about 1000--800 Ma and is probably roughly equivalent to the Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops. APW paths, loops, reversed polari- ty zones and pole positions, combined with geological data, permit definition of several markers that are useful in regional correlation. These form the basis for a proposed strati- graphic subdivision of the middle and upper Proterozoic in China. A tentative palaeogeo- graphic map has been drawn for the North China and Yangzi Blocks for the period fr

- tematic studies of late Precambrian rocks ranging in age from 1900 Ma to 600 Ma. These studies have been carried out at Jixian, Yangzi Gorges, Shennongjia and in the Fuzhou area where there is good exposure and the structure is relatively simple. These sections are suitable for measurement of remanent magnetization in the rocks. They are also the stratotype and para- stratotype sections for middle and upper Proterozoic rocks in China (Chen Jinbiao et al., 1980; Wang, Yulen et al., 1980; Zhao Zigiang et al., 1980; Chen Jinbiao et al,, 1981). 0301-9268/85/$03.30 © 1985 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. They do suggest, how- ever, that palaeomagnetic and magnetostratigraphic data have great poten- tial for resolving problems in Precambrian stratigraphy and tectonics. TECTONICS, VOL. 3, NO. 2, PAGES 179-200, APRIL 1984 PALEOMAGNETIC ASSESSMENT OF OROFLEXURAL DEFORMATION IN WEST-CENTRAL NEVADA AND SIGNIFICANCE FOR EMPLACEMENT OF ALLOCHTHONOUS ASSEMBLAGES John W. Geissman and James T. Callian Department of Geology, Colorado School of Mines John S. Oldow Department of Geology, Rice University Stephan E. Humphries Department of Geology, Colorado School of Mines Abstract. Abrupt westerly deflections of north-south trending facies boundari

west- central Basin and Range Province, have been explained by (1) post-Early Jurassic oroflexural folding and shear, (2) the existence of a pre-Late Jurassic resistant block along the western continental mar- gin, possibly representing late Precambrian breakup, and (3) regional flexure (\"Mina deflection\") prior to in- trusion of Late Cretaceous plutons which crosscut flexure-related structural trends. Paleomagnetic data gathered from Late Cretaceous plutons and remagnetized metasedimentary rocks along and north of the northern margin of the zone of east- west structural trends are not in support of significant oroflexural folding (and attending major clockwise rotation) since Late Cretaceous time

Samples were collected at two sites in the pluton itself and at one site in metasomatized calc-silicate and marble units at the contact (Figure 3). All samples from the pluton contain a magnetization of north- erly declination and steep to moderate positive inclination, which is removed over moderate peak fields and distributed temperatures (Figures 5e, 5f). Samples of the contact units contain similar com- ponents of magnetization, but their magne- tization properties (higher coercivities and blocking temperatures) are different from those of the Gunmetal pluton samples. All magnetization data are plotted in Figure 6c. The directions obtained from the contact units are statistically in- distinguishable from data from the intru- sive, implying that the host units have been at least locally remagnetized. The normal polarity of the characteristic magnetization is consistent with emplace- ment of the pluton during the Cretaceous Long Normal interval. While the paleomagnetic data from each locality are well grouped close to a time- averaged axial dipole field direction, several aspects of the data and the units sampled suggest that the characteristic magnetizations indeed reflect intrusive events in this area in Late Cretaceous time. The data may be used to infer amounts of Late Cretaceous and younger de- formation in the area. First, each pluton and the associated magnetic mineralogy is at most only slightly altered. Any systematic rotation of directions could presumably be ascribed to oro- flexural deformation postdating the plu- tons. We emphasize that the present analysis investigates the possibility of oroflexural deformation only in post-Late Cretaceous time. Earlier components of deformation cannot be evaluated with mag- netization data from Cretaceous plutons. The effectiveness of this study hinges on whether local structural elements related to Basin and Range extension (e.g., simple tilting of crustal blocks) can be differ- entiated from rotational components that might be associated with the formation of the Mina deflection. We will address this question in detail in the discussion section. Our observations largely support a primary, nonoroflexure/rotation origin for the geometry of the Mina deflection. They have clear and significant ramifica- tions for Paleozoic and Mesozoic tectonism and palcogeography in west-central Nevada. We have no doubt that local, shear-related deformation may have occurred in at least portions of the Basin and Range. Gillett and Van Alstine [1982a, b] have documented local rotation of crustal blocks forming the Desert Range and have related the deformation to Tertiary dextral slip along the Las Vegas shear zone. We assume that the plunge of the fold was acquired after folding because there is no evidence of regional tilting prior to Cretaceous folding and because the strain analysis work of Oldow 981a] has shown that fold axes were generally formed in a horizontal orientation. The tilt component of deformation was thus re- moved before the limbs were restored to the horizontal. The order of the exercise is actually insignificant; the value of k for the in situ data is 12.4, while k = 2.0 for the structurally corrected data set. An F ratio test establishes that the fold test for the E-xcelsior Mountains fold is negative at the 99.9% confidence level. The stratigraphic interval of the Columbia River basalt group that is the focus of this investigation consists of the lower flows of the Frenchmans Springs member [Mackin, 1961] of the Wanapum basalt formation (Figure 1). This process of distributed shear is similar to that proposed by Beck [1980] to explain tectonic transport of displaced crustal fragments of the Cordillera. However, in this case, the zone of distributed shear is within the Ginkgo flows of the Wanapum Basalt member rather than between discontinuous crustal fragments. The hypothesis that there is distrib- uted shear throughout the Columbia Plateau, southwestern Washington, and the Oregon coast requires that the structural geology of this region be fairly complex. Structural elements that may have facili- tated this deformation are numerous and include (1) abundant north and northwest trending dextral strike slip faults of the Columbia Plateau and adjacent Cascade Range [Bentley and Anderson, 1979] and (2) east to northeast trending folds in the same area [Bentley, 1977, 1980; Campbell and Bentley, 1981]. Movement on these structures has been continuous since 16 m.y.B.P. with major pulses at 14-13 m.y.B.P. and 9-7 m.y.B.P. [Bentley et al., 1980]. he Ginkgo flows, with their anomalous paleomagnetic direction and large areal distribution, provide the necessary paleomagnetic data to support the hypothesis that distributed shear has also contributed to tectonic rotations of the Pacific Northwest. In summary, paleomagnetic data from the Ginkgo flows of the Columbia River basalt Group suggest the prevailing tec- tonic mechanism for Columbia River Plateau and Oregon and Washington coast deformation, at least since 14 m.y.B.P., may well be southwestward increasing clockwise rotation about a nearby verti- cal axis, not a simple rotation of one large tectonic block. section_candidates.excerpt: C NORTHWEST Kenneth F. Fox, Jr. U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, Colorado Myrl E. Beck, Jr. U.S. Geological Survey and Department of Geology, Western Washington University, Bellingham Abstract. The direction of remanent magnetization for 102 sites in Eocene volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks of the O'Brien Creek Formation, Sanpoll Volcanics, and Klondike Mountain Formation suggests approximately 25 ø of clockwise rotation of a 100 by 200 km area in northeastern Washington. The volcanic rocks consist chiefly of rhyodacite and quartz latite flows, with intercalated ash flow tuff and volcaniclastic layers. These rocks have been sampled at 102 sites distributed among five volcanotectonic depressions: the Toroda Creek, Republic, Keller, and First Thought grabens and the Spokane-Enterprise lineament. The volcanic rocks probably range in age from 55 m.y. to about 48 m.y., and the 50- to 48-m.y.-old volcanic rocks within this suite appear to be rotated as much as the older rocks. Previous investigators have shown that 40-m.y.-old and younger plutonic rocks of northwestern Washington are not rotated; hence we infer that the north-central Washington rocks were rotated to their present declination between 48 and 40 m.y.B.P. (during the middle and/or late Eocene).

Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. The next higher stratigraphic unit is the Yojoa Group, consisting of a shaly lime- stone, the Cantarranas Formation (Neo- ccmian to Early AptJan) and a thick, mas- sive-bedded micrite/bicmicrite, the Atima Formation (AptJan and Albian). Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: TECTONICS, VOL. 4, NO. 6, PAGES 565-585, OCTOBER 1985 PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS FROM HONDURAS AND THEIR BEARING ON CARIBBEAN TECTONICS Wulf A. Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. POLARITY OF MAGNETIZATION Before the data can be used for tec- tonic interpretations, it is mandatory to establish the polarity of magnetization, for it determines the sense of rotation and the paleolatitude. Most of the sam- pled rock units are of AptJan through Cenomanian age, i.e., they were deposited during a period of constant normal mag- netic polarity (84-118 m.y., Harland et al. [1982]). All but three of the sedi- mentary sites are of the same polarity, which thus must be normal. One reversed horizon was encountered in the Atima Formation at its type locality (site A5). Gose Department of Geological Sciences and Institute for Geophysics University of Texas at Austin Abstract. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 37 sites in central and western Honduras and one site in north- western Nicaragua. The rocks are lime- stones, sandstones, and granites and range in age from 140 to 60 m.y. Regional fold- tests demonstrate that the rocks carry a prefolding (pre-Laramide) magnetization. The data indicate a very large clockwise rotation of the sampling area during the Early Cretaceous followed by a counter- clockwise rotation in the Late Cretaceous. The changes in latitude are minor during this time period. It is highly unlikely that these large rotations apply to the entire Car ibbean plate. Rather, they reflect the motion of a smaller area known as the Chortis Block. This interpretation is supported by paleomagnetic data from neighboring areas. POLARITY OF MAGNETIZATION Before the data can be used for tec- tonic interpretations, it is mandatory to establish the polarity of magnetization, for it determines the sense of rotation and the paleolatitude. Most of the sam- pled rock units are of AptJan through Cenomanian age, i.e., they were deposited during a period of constant normal mag- netic polarity (84-118 m.y., Harland et al. [1982]). All but three of the sedi- mentary sites are of the same polarity, which thus must be normal. One reversed horizon was encountered in the Atima Formation at its type locality (site A5). Its paleontological age of Upper AptJan (113-115 m.y.) suggests that this reversal may correspond to seafloor magnetic anomaly M0 (118-119 m.y., Harland et al. [1982] ). The other two reversed sites are from one stratigraphic horizon in the upper Valle de Angeles red beds (sites Vll, V12) which could correspond to any of the reversals younger than the long normal interval. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Late Precambrian and Early Paleozoic geological sequence preserved in Cape Breton Island, summarized in Figures 1 and 2, comprises Late Hadrynian basement volcanics and granites overlain by well- preserved Cambrian to Lower Ordovician shallow-water marine clastics and volcanics. The lithologic and faunal characteristics of these rocks and their correlation with similar strata found along strike in the northern Appalachians, particularly in eastern Newfoundland (see Figure la), have been discussed by many authors [e.g., Henningsmoen, 1969; Rast et al., 1976; Williams, 1978]. The assemblage of often geographically separate localities where similar rocks occur has been called the Avalon terrane by Williams and Hatcher [1983], named after the Avalon peninsula of Newfoundland. The Cambrian volcanics present in the Boisdale Peninsula (Bourinot Group) were the principal focus of our study. These volcanics comprise flows and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks, which appear to have had a restricted areal extent at the time they were formed [Keppie and Dostal, 1980; Hutchinson, 1952]. Interbedded volcanics and sediments of the Bourinot Group (Mid- Cambrian) in central Cape Breton Island were studied as part of a paleomagnetic investigation to quantify the geologically plausible displacements of the Avalon terrane with respect to the North American craton. Both volcanics and sediments reveal prefolding magnetizations with steep to intermediate inclinations. Dual- polarity magnetizations in different volcanic flows are probably primary and they yield a mean direction of D=293 ø, I=-66 ø (N=9, k=41.8, 95=8.1 ø) . The sediments reveal, upon detailed thermal demagnetization, complex multivectorial remanences. However, a few samples show characteristic components and a large number of samples (38) have intersecting great-circle remagnetization trajectories; when combined, this yields a mean direction of D=267 ø, I=-65 ø (k=16, mean radius of error ellipse is 8.5 ø ) .
